questions.prompt: A @Transactional method called from another method in the same class doesn't roll back. Why?
options: @Transactional only works on methods declared in an interface.
The transaction manager isn't configured.
Spring's proxy sits outside the object — a self-call goes straight to the target and never passes through the advice.
Rollback only happens for checked exceptions.
questions.explanation: Proxy-based AOP is invisible to the object itself. The fix is to move the transactional method into another bean, or self-inject. The checked-exception option is the good distractor — it's a real gotcha, but backwards: Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions by default and leaves checked ones alone.

questions.prompt: Listing 1,000 campaigns fires 1,001 queries. The entity has a @OneToMany collection.
options: @OneToMany defaults to EAGER, so each row loads its collection.
The entity is missing @Cacheable.
MySQL can't join on this relationship.
The collection is lazy and something touches it once per row — a join fetch or an entity graph collapses it to one query.
questions.explanation: @OneToMany is LAZY by default, so the N+1 comes from the code that iterates and reads. Serialising entities straight to JSON is the classic trigger — the serialiser touches every collection. Fetch what you need in one query, or project into a DTO so nothing lazy is reachable.

questions.prompt: This came up in review. The author says it works fine.
options: @Service should be @Component.
Field injection: the object can exist in an invalid state, the dependencies are invisible from the constructor, and unit-testing it needs reflection or a running container.
The injected fields should be static.
run() is missing @Transactional.
questions.explanation: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and lets the fields be final. The practical tell is testing: a constructor takes fakes in one line, whereas field injection means the test has to reach in and set them. It also hides growth — a class quietly acquiring its eighth @Autowired field would have been obvious as an eight-argument constructor.

questions.prompt: You own a service sending billions of messages a month. What do you put in place before you need it?
options: Metrics on what actually fails — queue depth, delivery latency percentiles, error rate broken down by downstream provider — and alerts on symptoms users feel rather than on CPU.
A runbook for the on-call engineer.
More logging around the delivery path.
Headroom: run bigger instances than you need.
questions.explanation: Operational ownership means knowing something is wrong before a customer tells you, and knowing where. Alerting on CPU produces pages nobody can act on; alerting on p99 delivery latency and per-provider error rate points at the problem. A runbook is genuinely valuable and it's the second thing — it's no use if nothing wakes you.

questions.prompt: Why might this Spring transaction not roll back as the author expects?
options: Transactions cannot call repositories.
RuntimeException never triggers rollback.
The annotation belongs on the repository interface only.
The internal self-call bypasses the proxy that applies @Transactional, so saveBatch may execute without the intended transaction boundary.
questions.explanation: Proxy-based transaction advice runs when a call crosses the proxy. A method calling another method on the same instance does not cross it. Move the boundary to an externally invoked method or another bean, and test the actual rollback behavior.
